title: Regression Metrics
html:
Regression metrics measure how far predictions are from the true values. They differ in how they punish large errors, in their units, and in what baseline they compare against.

MetricFormulaUnitsNotes
MAEmean |y − ŷ|Target'sEvery unit of error counts the same; less sensitive to outliers than MSE
MSEmean (y − ŷ)²Target's squaredPunishes large errors heavily; the usual training loss
RMSE√MSETarget'sLike MSE but interpretable; always ≥ MAE
R²1 − SS_res / SS_totUnitlessShare of variance explained relative to predicting the mean
Adjusted R²1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − p − 1)UnitlessPenalises extra predictors
MAPEmean |y − ŷ| / |y|%Scale-free, but undefined at y = 0, explodes near 0, asymmetric
RMSLERMSE of log(1 + y)≈ relativeFor targets spanning orders of magnitude; penalises under-prediction more
Median absolute errormedian |y − ŷ|Target'sRobust to a few huge errors
SS_res = Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² SS_tot = Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)² R² = 1 − SS_res / SS_tot

R² can be negative

R² compares the model with always predicting the mean of the true values. A model worse than that baseline has R² < 0 — common on a test set when a model has overfit or the data has drifted. R² = 1 is perfect; there is no lower bound.

MAE vs RMSE, and the MAPE trap

ChooseWhen
MAEErrors cost proportionally; outliers shouldn't dominate; you want the median-type prediction
RMSELarge errors are disproportionately bad; matches a squared-error training loss
R²Communicating fit relative to a naive baseline (always report an error metric too)
MAPE / sMAPE / WAPEStakeholders think in percentages and actuals are far from 0 (WAPE = Σ|e| / Σ|y| is more stable)
RMSLETargets such as prices or counts spanning orders of magnitude
Can R² be negative?

Yes. R² = 1 − SS_res/SS_tot, and if the model's squared errors exceed those of predicting the mean of the true values, it is below 0. On training data with an intercept, OLS can't do worse than the mean, but on test data any model can.

MAE or RMSE?

RMSE squares errors before averaging, so it penalises large errors more and is sensitive to outliers; MAE treats all errors linearly. Pick the one that matches the cost of errors in the business. RMSE ≥ MAE always; a large gap signals a few big errors.
